<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs<span class="ltx_pubnotes"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_thanks"><span class="ltx_note_name">Thanks: </span>Accepted at PNAS Nexus. Corresponding author: Marios Papachristou (<span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mpapachr@asu.edu</span>).</span></span></span></h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Marios Papachristou
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_note"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Note: </span>Department of Information Systems, W.P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA and Department of Computer Science, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY, USA. 
<br class="ltx_break">Supported by a scholarship from the Onassis Foundation (Scholarship ID: F ZT 056-1/2023-2024), and in part by a Simons Investigator Award, a Vannevar Bush Faculty Fellowship, AFOSR grant FA9550-19-1-0183, a Simons Collaboration grant, and a grant from the MacArthur Foundation.
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yuan Yuan
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_note"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Note: </span>Graduate School of Management, University of California Davis, Davis, CA, USA.
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Social networks profoundly influence how humans form opinions, exchange information, and organize collectively. As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded into social and professional environments, it is critical to understand whether their interactions approximate human-like network dynamics. We develop a framework to study the network formation behaviors of multiple LLM agents and benchmark them against human decisions. Across synthetic and real-world settings, including friendship, telecommunication, and employment networks, we find that LLMs consistently reproduce fundamental micro-level principles such as preferential attachment, triadic closure, and homophily, as well as macro-level properties including community structure and small-world effects. Importantly, the relative emphasis of these principles adapts to context: for example, LLMs favor homophily in friendship networks but heterophily in organizational settings, mirroring patterns of social mobility. A controlled human-subject survey confirms strong alignment between LLMs and human participants in link-formation decisions. These results establish that LLMs can serve as powerful tools for social simulation and synthetic data generation, while also raising critical questions about bias, fairness, and the design of AI systems that participate in human networks.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p"><em id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Keywords:</em> social networks, network formation, large language models, computational social science</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p"><em id="abstract1.3.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Code:</em> <a href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16969696" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16969696</a></p>
    
<p id="abstract1.4" class="ltx_p"><em id="abstract1.4.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Data:</em> <a href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17196412" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17196412</a></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Introduction</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent progress in large language models (LLMs),
such as GPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>, Claude <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, and Llama <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>, have shown promising developments in AI techniques and their integration into real-life applications. It is thus crucial to comprehend AI actions to ensure they align with human expectations, mitigate potential risks, and maximize their benefits. Misaligned AI actions may lead to unintended consequences, such as biased decision-making, fairness issues, and the miscoordinative or non-cooperative behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>. Recently, researchers have started to apply social science methodologies, such as methods analogous to laboratory experiments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, agent-based modeling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, and qualitative methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, to study LLMs. These methods not only reveal the capabilities and interpretability of LLMs but also suggest their potential for applications in social science <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In human societies, social networks play a crucial role in shaping individual behaviors, preferences, and connections, as well as influencing the diffusion of information and norms across communities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite>.
LLMs have shown great potential in social contexts, notably as intelligent personal assistants that facilitate social and prosocial interactions (see, e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>). However, less is known about how LLMs’ behaviors and preferences align with human network formation principles <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>.
This is particularly crucial, as it sheds light on the potential of these models to shape and be shaped by the networks of human relationships, which is a fundamental aspect of social systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, there has been an emerging body of work regarding LLM-based agent-based models, where the research community has devised frameworks for social simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, and have shown that collectives of LLMs exhibit linguistic collective biases <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, and the friendship paradox <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, showing that LLMs are promising at simulating real-world social networks.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our study complements these works, and explores LLMs’ behaviors and preferences in the context of network formation with both synthetic and real-world social networks, and answers the question <em id="Sx1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">“Which complex phenomena emerge by interactions between multiple LLMs?”</em> beyond merely focusing on the modeling and simulation aspect. By analyzing such interactions, we aim to understand the implications of LLMs representing humans in social and professional settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, we examine micro-level social network properties including preferential attachment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, triadic closure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, and homophily <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, as well as macro-level properties including community structure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, and the small-world phenomenon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">By analyzing LLM agents interacting dynamically in several different contexts and environments, with a variety of models (both closed and open-weight), and variations of the prompts, we find that in synthetic network simulations, LLMs displayed preferential attachment, homophily, and triadic closure, resulting in the formation of community structures and small-world dynamics.
More notably, in real-world social network simulations, we find that LLMs prioritize triadic closure and homophily over preferential attachment when forming new links, indicating a strong preference for connecting with similar nodes or shared acquaintances. Additionally, in a telecommunication network, LLMs tended to prioritize homophily and preferential attachment over triadic closure, and in a company network, the agents who corresponded to employees formed links frequently with managers, which showcases behavior that is consistent with human social mobility principles.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Generally, LLMs not only exhibit fundamental social network formation principles in synthetic simulations but also adapt their strategies based on the context of real-world networks, mirroring human social behaviors specific to each setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">As LLM technology continues to evolve, our study serves as an early exploration of their potential in social network studies, with several significant implications for future studies.
First, our study demonstrates the potential of LLMs for agent-based modeling. By simulating decision-making processes that approximate human-like behavior across various network settings, LLMs can provide valuable insights into the emergence of social phenomena. Although these models are still in early stages of development, they offer an intriguing framework for studying and designing systems that can mimic key aspects of real-world dynamics. This opens up possibilities for applying LLMs to explore and understand complex behaviors in social, professional, and collaborative environments.
Second, our work highlights the potential of LLMs for synthetic dataset generation, a critical area in network science. Although the accuracy of LLM-based predictions is not yet perfect, like all other link prediction models, this approach is particularly valuable in scenarios where privacy concerns limit access to real-world data. By simulating realistic datasets that capture important network properties, LLMs can facilitate research and experimentation without compromising sensitive information.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2402.10659v7/principle_1.png" id="Sx1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:429/507;" width="429" height="507" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="Sx1.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results for Principle 1 (preferential attachment)</span> The multi-LLM setup was given neighborhood information <math id="Sx1.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{N_{j,t}:j\in V_{t}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{N_{j,t}:j\in V_{t}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. <span id="Sx1.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a, b):</span> Probability of connecting to top-<math id="Sx1.F1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-degree nodes for varying model (temperature is fixed to 1.0 and environment to baseline), temperature (model fixed to GPT-3.5 and environment to baseline) and environment (model fixed to GPT-3.5 and environment temperature to 1.5) for networks generated according to Principle 1 with <math id="Sx1.F1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=200</annotation></semantics></math> nodes. (a) shows the whole range of <math id="Sx1.F1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, and (b) shows the top <math id="Sx1.F1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-2.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-2.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> nodes. <span id="Sx1.F1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c):</span> Power Law exponents and standard errors for varying model, temperature, and environment.
<span id="Sx1.F1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d):</span> Simulated networks. </section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Results</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this study, we investigated whether LLMs exhibit fundamental principles of network formation observed in human social networks. By simulating multiple LLM agents acting independently within separate conversational threads, we examined their behaviors in decision-making scenarios involving network connections.
We focused on three micro-level network principles – preferential attachment, triadic closure, and homophily – and two macro-level phenomena–community structure and the small-world effect. To assess the robustness of our findings, we varied the temperature settings of different LLM models, including GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o Mini, Llama 3 (70b-instruct), and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. We also experimented with different environmental prompts (e.g., friendship, collaboration, community) to test prompt sensitivity.
Additionally, we employed an interview-like method to probe the LLMs’ decision-making rationale and conducted experiments using Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite> (the experiments are deferred to <a href="#S4" title="D Chain-of-Thought Experiments ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>). Finally, we extended our analysis to real-world networks, including a social media friendship network, a telecommunication network, and a company collaboration network, to compare the network formation preferences between LLMs and humans.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">More information about the experimental procedure, methods, and materials can be found in the <a href="#S1" title="A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="Sx2.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Micro-Level Properties</h3>

<section id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Principle 1: Preferential Attachment</h4>

<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Preferential attachment is a fundamental concept in network science, illustrating how nodes in a network gain connections over time, leading to a scale-free degree distribution characterized by a few highly connected nodes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To test if LLM agents exhibit preferential attachment, we simulated network growth by sequentially adding nodes to an initially empty network. Each new node was prompted with information about existing nodes, and the person to connect with was decided. We generated networks with <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=200</annotation></semantics></math> nodes to observe meaningful degree distributions<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              Note that we provide the full network structure in the prompt, so models are not inherently biased toward forming links with the highest-degree nodes.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On a micro-scale, <a href="#Sx1.F1" title="In Introduction ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> illustrates the probability of connecting to a top-<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> node as a function of its degree percentile (<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k/n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k/n</annotation></semantics></math>). To demonstrate the tendency toward preferential attachment, we compare these probabilities to a null model assuming random connections (represented by dashed lines), where the likelihood of connecting to a top-<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> node is simply <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k/n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k/n</annotation></semantics></math>.
Our findings reveal that all models prefer connecting to higher-degree nodes. Notably, GPT-3.5 exhibits a weaker preference, while other, arguably more capable models, show an even stronger inclination toward preferential attachment. Using GPT-3.5 as an example, we examine the effect of temperature – a parameter controlling the variability of model output – on this tendency. At lower temperatures, the model makes fewer stochastic choices and, as a result, is more likely to connect to high-degree nodes.
We also vary the prompt to explore the influence of “environment”-contextual settings such as school, work, or community. The results show slight variations compared to the baseline (GPT-3.5 with temperature = 1.5), yet the tendency for preferential attachment persists across environments.
In all cases, the observed curves lie above the null model, underscoring the presence of preferential attachment.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we investigate the degree distribution of the resulting graphs. As shown in <a href="#Sx1.F1" title="In Introduction ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the resulting networks display a pattern where a few nodes have many connections while most have few, indicative of a scale-free distribution, with form:</p>
<table id="Sx2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="Sx2.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="Sx2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\pi(d)\propto d^{-\gamma},\quad\text{where}\quad\gamma&gt;1." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mtext>where</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\pi(d)\propto d^{-\gamma},\quad\text{where}\quad\gamma&gt;1.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">We estimated the exponent <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> for different models and temperatures. Our analysis reveals several notable patterns in the networks generated by LLM agents under different conditions. First, models newer than GPT-3.5 exhibit a slightly larger <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>γ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> than GPT-3.5. This implies that these models display a stronger tendency toward preferential attachment and the formation of hubs.
Second, as the temperature increases the power-law exponent <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>γ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> generally becomes larger. This indicates that higher temperatures introduce more variance in node connectivity, leading to degree distributions with heavier tails. Third, the environmental context significantly affects the value of <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>γ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, when the network is framed within a “school” environment, the exponent increases, suggesting a more uniform distribution of connections and fewer highly central nodes.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, while the prompts we have utilized thus far have provided the model with the complete existing network structure, we also explore an alternative scenario: what happens if agents are supplied solely with the degree of other alternatives, without access to the network’s full structure? As detailed in <a href="#S3" title="C Network Evolution and Omitted Simulations ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>, our findings reveal that limiting agents to degree information alone also leads to notable structural differences in the networks that emerge (cf <a href="#S3.F3" title="In Simulations with Degree Information ‣ C.1 Principle 1: Preferential Attachment ‣ C Network Evolution and Omitted Simulations ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">SI.3</span></a>). Thus, degree information alone yields more restrictive structures than providing the agents with the full topological information (i.e., the neighbors).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The findings highlight the practical potential of LLMs in modeling complex networks, such as social, economic, or biological systems, by leveraging their ability to simulate preferential attachment and scale-free distributions. These models can be used to study real-world phenomena like information diffusion, hub formation, or connectivity patterns under varying conditions. Additionally, the sensitivity of network structures to parameters like temperature and context underscores the importance of prompt design in steering outcomes, making LLMs versatile tools for tailored simulations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Principle 2: Triadic Closure</h4>

<figure id="Sx2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.10659v7/principle_2.svg" id="Sx2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:333/443;" width="333" height="443"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="Sx2.F2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results for Principle 2 (triadic closure).</span> <span id="Sx2.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a, b):</span> Probability of connecting to top-<math id="Sx2.F2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> nodes (in terms of common neighbors) for varying model (temperature is fixed to 1.0 and environment to baseline), temperature (model fixed to GPT-4 Mini and environment to baseline) and environment (model fixed to GPT-4 Mini and environment temperature to 0.5) for networks generated according to Principle 2 (<math id="Sx2.F2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math>, 10 simulations for each model, environment and temperature). The dotted diagonal line corresponds to the null model, where connections are made at random. Panel (a) shows top-<math id="Sx2.F2.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="Sx2.F2.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="Sx2.F2.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> in the range <math id="Sx2.F2.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10-50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10-50\%</annotation></semantics></math>, and Panel (b) shows top-<math id="Sx2.F2.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="Sx2.F2.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> in the range of <math id="Sx2.F2.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10-100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10-100\%</annotation></semantics></math>. <span id="Sx2.F2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c):</span> Marginal transitivity (<math id="Sx2.F2.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>) and probability of an edge within a community (<math id="Sx2.F2.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math>) for networks generated according to Principle 2 in different models, temperatures, and environments. The dotted line corresponds to the random null model. <span id="Sx2.F2.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d):</span> The figure shows the resulting networks created by GPT-4 Mini, according to Principle 2 when the intersection of the neighborhoods of the query node and each alternative is provided and comparison of the metrics <math id="Sx2.F2.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.F2.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math> with the random null model. The node colors correspond to the groups to which each node belongs. The bold edges (red or blue) correspond to the newly created inter-cluster edges, and the orange edges correspond to the new intra-cluster edges. <span id="Sx2.F2.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(e, f):</span> Marginal transitivity (<math id="Sx2.F2.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>) and network instances when the initial network is an Erdös-Rényi graph with <math id="Sx2.F2.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.F2.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The second micro-level principle we examine is triadic closure, which posits that individuals are more likely to form connections with friends of friends, thus creating closed triads in the network. This process strengthens network structure and cohesion, grounded in the idea that two nodes are more likely to connect if they share a common neighbor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To investigate triadic closure, we employ an assortative stochastic block model (SBM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> to create an initial network <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> nodes divided into two equal-sized clusters <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>. Connections within each cluster are formed with a probability of <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>, while inter-cluster connections occur with a probability of <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1</annotation></semantics></math>. This setup mirrors our assumption that nodes within the same cluster are more inclined to connect due to a higher number of shared neighbors. In subsequent time steps, we then examine each node <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, considering the intersection of neighborhoods of <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>’s non-neighbors<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              Similar outcomes arise when providing neighbors instead of common neighbors.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted ten simulations with <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math> nodes to facilitate clear visualization and ensure statistical significance<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              Choosing <math id="footnote3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math> instead of a larger number like <math id="footnote3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=200</annotation></semantics></math> aids in visualization and maintains statistical significance.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">On a micro-scale, <a href="#Sx2.F2" title="In Principle 2: Triadic Closure ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the probability of connecting to a top-<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-percentile node as a function of the number of common neighbors. The dashed lines represent the results of null models, where connections are chosen randomly; which corresponds to the probability of connecting to a top-<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> percentile node in terms of the common neighbors being <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k/n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k/n</annotation></semantics></math>. Our findings reveal that, across all models, there is a consistently higher probability of forming links with nodes that share more common neighbors. Unlike the behavior observed in preferential attachment, temperature does not appear to severely impact this probability. This tendency to form links with nodes that have more common neighbors is consistent across various contexts, including school, work, and community environments. These results suggest that the triadic closure tendency is a robust phenomenon, persisting across different model families, configurations, and environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Then, for evaluating triadic closure on the network (macroscopic) level, we utilize two metrics: <span id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">marginal transitivity</span> and <span id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">probability of edge formation within the same community</span>. Marginal transitivity (<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>) represents the change in the ratio of closed triangles to all triads, transitioning from the SBM-generated network <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> to the final network <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> after <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=50</annotation></semantics></math> iterations:</p>
<table id="Sx2.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="Sx2.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="Sx2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle D=3\times\frac{\text{\# triangles}(G_{T})}{\text{\# triads}(G_{T})}-3\times\frac{\text{\# triangles}(G_{1})}{\text{\# triads}(G_{1})}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mtext># triangles</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext># triads</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mtext># triangles</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mtext># triads</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle D=3\times\frac{\text{\# triangles}(G_{T})}{\text{\# triads}(G_{T})}-3\times\frac{\text{\# triangles}(G_{1})}{\text{\# triads}(G_{1})}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where a large positive <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> indicates a strong triadic closure tendency.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">As we investigate under SBM, the same community membership indicates more open triads being closed.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Marginal transitivity (<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>), presented in <a href="#Sx2.F2" title="In Principle 2: Triadic Closure ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, demonstrates a statistically significant increase across all models, temperatures, and environments, underscoring the robust nature of triadic closure.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#Sx2.F2" title="In Principle 2: Triadic Closure ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, sample networks from GPT-3.5 are displayed, with the upper panel showing networks where the entire structure is provided and the lower panel showing those with only common neighbor numbers provided. Nodes are color-coded to indicate their cluster memberships in the SBM, with red and blue edges within clusters and orange edges between clusters. Newly formed edges are highlighted with thicker lines.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, to eliminate the possibility that the results are due to structural bias from the initial structure (SBM), we note that we can obtain the same results when we start from a more “neutral” initial topology. Specifically, we get the same results and an even stronger effect for the marginal transitivity (<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>) by starting from a sparse Erdös-Rényi graph with <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math> nodes and <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>. We find that, across or models, temperatures and variations of the prompts, the resulting network exhibits higher marginal transitivity (<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>) compared to the random null model, which makes connections at random starting from the same Erdös-Rényi graph, and the results are statistically significant (cf. <a href="#Sx2.F2" title="In Principle 2: Triadic Closure ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>; <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>; t-test comparing the marginal transitivity of the resulting LLM-generated networks and the random null model).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, these findings show that most LLMs exhibit a consistent tendency for triadic closure across various configurations, temperatures, and environments. This behavior mirrors human network dynamics, highlighting the models’ ability to simulate realistic social and structural networks and reinforcing their alignment with social principles observed in real-world communities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Principle 3: Homophily</h4>

<figure id="Sx2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2402.10659v7/principle_3.png" id="Sx2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:429/376;" width="429" height="376" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="Sx2.F3.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results for Principle 3 (Homophily) and Principle 4 (Community structure due to homophily)</span>. <span id="Sx2.F3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a):</span> Assortativity and Louvain modularity by Principle 3 (<math id="Sx2.F3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math>, 5 runs per row) across school, work, and community settings. All comparisons to the random null model (<math id="Sx2.F3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=0</annotation></semantics></math>) are statistically significant (<math id="Sx2.F3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.0003" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.0003</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.0003</annotation></semantics></math>, t-tests with Bonferroni correction for three tests). Modularity is also significantly greater than 0 (<math id="Sx2.F3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>).
<span id="Sx2.F3.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b):</span> Network examples and communities for GPT-3.5 agents. Compared to a null model where agents connect randomly (<math id="Sx2.F3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=0</annotation></semantics></math>).
<span id="Sx2.F3.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c):</span> Influence of distractor features (favorite color, lucky number) on homophily. Compared to a random null model with <math id="Sx2.F3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=0</annotation></semantics></math>. All results are statistically significant (<math id="Sx2.F3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.00025" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.00025</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.00025</annotation></semantics></math>), with Bonferroni correction over 3 tests (location, favorite color, hobby).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Homophily reflects the tendency for nodes with similar characteristics or attributes to form connections and associate with each other. This phenomenon is based on the principle that individuals in a network are more likely to connect with others who share similar traits, interests, or demographics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To test whether LLM agents exhibit homophily, we perform the following experiment: We generate nodes with randomly generated attributes regarding a hobby (randomly chosen among three hobbies), a favorite color (randomly chosen among three colors), and a location within the US (randomly chosen among three US locations) and provide the attributes of the other nodes and the node’s own attributes, and each node is tasked to form up to <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta=5</annotation></semantics></math> links with others. For each node <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, we provide it with the features <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> of all non-neighbors <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>. The seed network is taken to be the empty graph. We run ten simulations
for networks with <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50</annotation></semantics></math> nodes and <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta=5</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate homophily, we calculate the attribute assortativity coefficient for each of the features. For each property <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> which takes <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> distinct values <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{1},\dots,P_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{1},\dots,P_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> (indexed by <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>), its <span id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">assortativity coefficient <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math></span> is defined as</p>
<table id="Sx2.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="Sx2.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="Sx2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle R=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}M_{kk}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_{k}b_{k}}{1-\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_{k}b_{k}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle R=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}M_{kk}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_{k}b_{k}}{1-\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_{k}b_{k}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> represents the mixing matrix. Its elements <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{kl}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{kl}</annotation></semantics></math> reflect the proportion of edges connecting two nodes with values <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. We define <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{k}=\sum_{l=1}^{K}M_{kl}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{k}=\sum_{l=1}^{K}M_{kl}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{k}=\sum_{l=1}^{K}M_{lk}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{k}=\sum_{l=1}^{K}M_{lk}</annotation></semantics></math>. Assortativity ranges from <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+1</annotation></semantics></math>. A positive assortativity indicates nodes preferentially connect to similar ones, forming a homophilous network. Conversely, a negative assortativity suggests connections primarily occur between dissimilar nodes, indicating heterophily.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">From <a href="#Sx2.F3" title="In Principle 3: Homophily ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we observe that different attributes exhibit varying levels of assortativity. First, homophily is present across all LLMs, regardless of the specific model or configuration (e.g., temperature settings), all show positive assortativity for all four attributes, where they obtain statistically significant results <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.0003" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.0003</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.0003</annotation></semantics></math> (t-test with 0, Bonferroni correction across three tests across the three features). This aligns with human societies, where homophily is a primary driver of network formation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite><span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              As an additional robustness check, we also tested mutual agreement connections. In that setting, after a node <math id="footnote4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> is chosen by node <math id="footnote4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="footnote4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> has to confirm the creation of the link from itself to <math id="footnote4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="footnote4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\to i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\to i</annotation></semantics></math>). We ran several experiments with different models and temperatures and we found the results not to be affected, namely, the proposed connections were always bilateral.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, to test the effect of the features on homophily as indicated by the assortativity coefficient for each attribute, we introduce a <span id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distractor feature</span>, which corresponds to a lucky number that is randomly chosen between 0 and 9. We repeat the simulations for all models and measure the effect of each feature on <a href="#Sx2.F3" title="In Principle 3: Homophily ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. We still observe strong homophily effects with high statistical significance after applying Bonferroni correction for four tests (<math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.00025" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.00025</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.00025</annotation></semantics></math>, t-test with the random null model where connections are done at random which has assortativity <math id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=0</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">However, we show that lucky numbers consistently show lower assortativity coefficients, indicating they are less considered when forming homophilous connections. This is consistent with our prior expectation that humans typically do not prioritize shared lucky numbers when establishing relationships.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Surprisingly, even though the lucky number does not seem to impact homophily much, the favorite color exhibits a similar level of homophily as hobbies. One might expect that hobbies, being substantive interests, would have a stronger influence on social connections than favorite colors, which are more arbitrary preferences. However, this finding aligns with the social identity theory and the minimal group paradigm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>. According to this paradigm, even minimal and arbitrary group distinctions – such as a preference for certain colors – can lead to in-group favoritism and influence social connections. This suggests that LLM agents, akin to humans, may form connections based on even trivial shared attributes, reflecting inherent tendencies toward group formation based on minimal commonalities.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.SSSx3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">All in all, LLMs can capture and reproduce subtle human social behaviors, not just linguistic patterns. This underscores their potential as powerful tools for social simulation. However, these findings may also raise important considerations regarding bias, fairness, and the ethical design of AI systems (cf. Discussion Section).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Macro-Level Principles</h3>

<section id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Principle 4: Community Structure</h4>

<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The community structure of networks refers to the organization of nodes or individuals within a network into distinct and densely interconnected groups or clusters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>.
Identifying community structures is crucial for understanding the overall dynamics of a network, as it reveals patterns of relationships and interactions that might not be apparent at the global level.<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              As an example, we present only the results from GPT-3.5 for Principle 4 (Community Structure) and Principle 5 (Small-World).</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Both triadic closure and homophily contribute to the formation of community structures. By examining how these two factors contribute to network formation, we aim to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms driving community dynamics in LLM-generated networks.
We employ the simulation results presented in the synthetic networks to determine whether community structure in networks generated by LLMs emerges from triadic closure or homophily.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">First, we consider the networks generated in <a href="#Sx2.F2" title="In Principle 2: Triadic Closure ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. We examine how LLM agents’ choices strengthen the network’s community structure.
Specifically, we leverage the fact that the SBM graph has a preexisting community structure and measure how the newly formed links reinforce such a structure. Visual inspection shows that the newly added links, represented by the bold edges, happen mostly within each cluster, reinforcing the community structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To measure the emergence of communities in the triadic closure case, we initially examine the probability of forming an edge within the same community (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math>). The quantity <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math> is calculated by the ratio of edges in <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{T}\setminus G_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>∖</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{T}\setminus G_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> (newly formed edges) connecting nodes within the same cluster:</p>
<table id="Sx2.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="Sx2.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="Sx2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\hat{p}=\frac{\left|\left\{\{i,j\}\in E(G_{T})\setminus E(G_{1}):y_{i}=y_{j}\right\}\right|}{\left|E(G_{T})\setminus E(G_{1})\right|}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∖</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∖</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hat{p}=\frac{\left|\left\{\{i,j\}\in E(G_{T})\setminus E(G_{1}):y_{i}=y_{j}\right\}\right|}{\left|E(G_{T})\setminus E(G_{1})\right|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i},y_{j}\in{A,B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i},y_{j}\in{A,B}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the community memberships of nodes <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. A value of <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math> exceeding <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math> suggests a triadic closure tendency and community structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#Sx2.F2" title="In Principle 2: Triadic Closure ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows that <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math> is significantly higher than 0.5 (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>, t-test compared to 0.5), and is significantly bigger compared to a random null model where connections are made at random. All in all, this indicates that most edges are within the same community, strengthening the community structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we investigate the community structure resulting from homophily using modularity maximization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. Modularity quantifies the discrepancy between the actual number of edges within communities and the expected number in a random network with identical node count and degree distribution, following the Chung-Lu model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>. This model presumes that nodes maintain their weighted degree, with edges randomly distributed. The weighted modularity <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> for a graph with edge weights <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> communities is defined as</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<table id="Sx2.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="Sx2.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="Sx2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle Q=\sum_{c=1}^{C}\left[\frac{L_{c}}{W}-r\left(\frac{k_{c}}{2W}\right)^{2}\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mi>W</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle Q=\sum_{c=1}^{C}\left[\frac{L_{c}}{W}-r\left(\frac{k_{c}}{2W}\right)^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> represents the total edge weights, <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> the intra-community link weights for community <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> the total weighted degree within community <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> the resolution parameter, set to 1 for our analysis. High modularity values (e.g., greater than 0.5) indicate significant community structuring, diverging from the random model.<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              Given the NP-Hard nature of maximizing <math id="footnote6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>, we employ the Louvain algorithm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> to approximate the highest possible modularity.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p9" class="ltx_para">
