<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Firstly, we note that when the experimental setting for Principle 2 (cf. <a href="#Sx2.F2" title="In Principle 2: Triadic Closure ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) is initialized with an SBM or an Erdös-Renyi network, we obtain positive modularity <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>; t-test comparing with 0).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Secondly, regarding the homophily experiment (cf. <a href="#Sx2.F3" title="In Principle 3: Homophily ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), for the network’s weights, we use the number of common attributes shared between each pair of nodes: <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{ij}=\left|\left\{k:x_{i}^{(k)}=x_{j}^{(k)}\right\}\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{ij}=\left|\left\{k:x_{i}^{(k)}=x_{j}^{(k)}\right\}\right|</annotation></semantics></math> for each link <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(i,j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(i,j)</annotation></semantics></math> in the final network. Here, <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p10.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{j}^{(k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{j}^{(k)}</annotation></semantics></math> correspond to the <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p10.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th features of <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p10.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p10.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#Sx2.F3" title="In Principle 3: Homophily ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, various colors represent the communities identified by the Louvain algorithm at different temperatures for GPT-3.5. Notably, communities appear more distinct at lower temperatures, likely due to reduced randomness in decision-making at these temperatures.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p12.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#Sx2.F3" title="In Principle 3: Homophily ‣ Micro-Level Properties ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the distribution of Louvain modularity values across simulations accross different LLM models and different environments, indicating consistent community structure with positive modularity at all temperatures, confirmed by a t-test against a modularity of <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q=0</annotation></semantics></math> for a random graph (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Our results demonstrate that community structures manifest in networks generated by LLMs, driven by both triadic closure and homophily.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Principle 5: Small-World</h4>

<figure id="Sx2.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2402.10659v7/principle_5.png" id="Sx2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/325;" width="476" height="325" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="Sx2.F4.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fitted results for Principle 5 (small world) for <math id="Sx2.F4.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.25,k=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.25,k=5</annotation></semantics></math> (a1-a3), <math id="Sx2.F4.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.5,k=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.5,k=5</annotation></semantics></math> (b1-b3), and <math id="Sx2.F4.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.75,k=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.75,k=5</annotation></semantics></math> (c1-c3).</span> <span id="Sx2.F4.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a1-c1):</span> <em id="Sx2.F4.14" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Average clustering coefficient</em> <math id="Sx2.F4.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> the <em id="Sx2.F4.15" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">average shortest path length</em> <math id="Sx2.F4.m37" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>. The comparison is made with respect to a Watts-Strogatz graph with <math id="Sx2.F4.m38" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=50,k=5,\beta\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0.25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.75</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=50,k=5,\beta\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}</annotation></semantics></math>. The error bars correspond to 95% confidence intervals. The results are compared against the Watts-Strogatz model with the same parameters <math id="Sx2.F4.m39" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.F4.m40" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> as a null model. The t-test comparing <math id="Sx2.F4.m41" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.F4.m42" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> for the LLM-generated networks and Watts-Strogatz networks yields <math id="Sx2.F4.m43" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&gt;0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&gt;0.05</annotation></semantics></math> (Bonferroni correction for two tests). <span id="Sx2.F4.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a2-c2):</span> Regression plots relating <em id="Sx2.F4.17" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">average shortest path length</em> (<math id="Sx2.F4.m44" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>) and <em id="Sx2.F4.18" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">average clustering coefficient</em> (<math id="Sx2.F4.m45" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>) with <math id="Sx2.F4.m46" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>. The value <math id="Sx2.F4.m47" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> in legends represents the effect size (slope of the regression lines). <span id="Sx2.F4.19" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a3-c3):</span> Estimated values <math id="Sx2.F4.m48" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="Sx2.F4.m49" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}</annotation></semantics></math> for LLM-generated networks based on matching the average clustering coefficient and difference in the average shortest path between LLM-generated networks and Watts-Strogatz with the <span id="Sx2.F4.20" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">estimated rewiring probability</span> <math id="Sx2.F4.m50" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> for GPT-3.5 agents. We report the <math id="Sx2.F4.m51" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>-values of the t-test comparing the average shortest path length of the LLM-generated networks and the average shortest path length of the Watts-Strogatz graphs with rewiring probability <math id="Sx2.F4.m52" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math>. <span id="Sx2.F4.21" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d):</span> Regression plot for the relation <math id="Sx2.F4.m53" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L\sim\log(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L\sim\log(n)</annotation></semantics></math> for different LLM models and environments (school, work, community) for <math id="Sx2.F4.m54" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.25</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.F4.m55" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=5</annotation></semantics></math>. The legend shows the effect size (<math id="Sx2.F4.m56" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>) and the <math id="Sx2.F4.m57" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>-value. The results are compared against the Watts-Strogatz model with the same parameters <math id="Sx2.F4.m58" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.F4.m59" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> as a null model. (*: <math id="Sx2.F4.m60" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.025" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.025</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.025</annotation></semantics></math>; **: <math id="Sx2.F4.m61" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.005" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.005</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.005</annotation></semantics></math>, and ***: <math id="Sx2.F4.m62" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.0005" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.0005</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.0005</annotation></semantics></math>, Bonferroni correction for two tests; <math id="Sx2.F4.m63" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.F4.m64" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>.).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The small-world phenomenon is characterized by networks where nodes are interconnected in tight clusters, yet the average distance between any two nodes remains relatively short, typically scaling logarithmically with the network size <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. This balance between high clustering and short path lengths characterizes small-world networks.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A small-world network is defined by its <span id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">average shortest path length <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math></span>, which grows logarithmically with the size of the network <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>,<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              As per the definition in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span> expressed as</p>
<table id="Sx2.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="Sx2.Ex5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="Sx2.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle L\sim\log(n)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle L\sim\log(n).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis utilizes the Watts-Strogatz model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite> as a benchmark to investigate whether LLMs can generate networks exhibiting small-world characteristics.
This model has a delicate balance between local clustering and short average path lengths: Nodes tend to form clusters or groups (triadic closure), exhibiting a high level of interconnectedness within these local neighborhoods, whereas at the same time, the existence of a few long-range connections ensures that the entire network is reachable with relatively few steps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We employ a modified version of the model, where edge rewiring is informed by LLM queries, based on the current network structure. The generation process is parametrized by the number of nodes (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>), average degree (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>), and the rewiring probability (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>). See details in <a href="#S1.SS2" title="A.2 Details for Small-World Experiments ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a></p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We generated networks of various sizes, ranging from <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=10</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=100</annotation></semantics></math>, to explore the relationship between the network size (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>) and two key metrics: the average shortest path length (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>) and the average clustering coefficient (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>). For this analysis, we considered values of <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> set at 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75, with a fixed <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=5</annotation></semantics></math> to serve as a consistent parameter.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">However, when directly compared with the Watts-Strogatz model, the networks generated by the LLMs do not precisely replicate the characteristics of Watts-Strogatz networks for the corresponding rewiring probabilities (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>). As illustrated in panels (a1-c1) of <a href="#Sx2.F4" title="In Principle 5: Small-World ‣ Macro-Level Principles ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we fail to reject the null hypothesis at level <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math> that the LLM-generated networks have the same average shortest path length as the Watts-Strogatz model for the rewiring probabilities (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>) of 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 (t-test comparing the average shortest path lengths, Bonferroni correction for two tests). Additionally, LLM-generated networks also fail to reject the null hypothesis at level <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math> that the LLM-generated networks have the same average clustering coefficient as the Watts-Strogatz model for the same rewiring probabilities <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> (Bonferroni correction for two tests). These results may suggest similarities in the network structure and connectivity patterns between the LLM-generated networks and the classical Watts-Strogatz model.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">We also provide regression analysis by examining the correlation between the average shortest path length and average clustering coefficient versus <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log(n)</annotation></semantics></math> (refer to <a href="#Sx2.F4" title="In Principle 5: Small-World ‣ Macro-Level Principles ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). We found that across all tested temperatures, the relationships were statistically significant, with most regressions yielding statistically significant results after applying Bonferroni correction for two tests (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.0005" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.0005</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.0005</annotation></semantics></math>). This indicates that the average shortest path length increases proportionally with <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log(n)</annotation></semantics></math>. Similarly, for the average clustering coefficient, we demonstrated that it inversely scales with <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/\log(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/\log(n)</annotation></semantics></math>, with the majority of regression analyses also showing high statistical significance after Bonferroni correction for the two tests (<math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.0005" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.0005</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.0005</annotation></semantics></math>). These findings align with the small-world properties of organizational networks as documented in the study by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, suggesting that these characteristics are not only prevalent but also predictable across different network sizes.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify how LLM-generated networks resemble Watts-Strogatz networks, we fit the estimated <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> values for each LLM-generated network.<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              We conducted a binary search to identify the <math id="footnote8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> values for which the Watts-Strogatz networks’ average clustering coefficients match those of the LLM-generated networks.</span></span></span>
In <a href="#Sx2.F4" title="In Principle 5: Small-World ‣ Macro-Level Principles ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we plot the estimated values for <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> for each value of <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> and each temperature. Here, <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>-values result from a t-test comparing with the average shortest path length of Watts-Strogatz with rewiring probability <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math>.
These results show that while the average shortest path lengths are not identical, they are sufficiently close, with the differences not being statistically significant at the <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1</annotation></semantics></math> level for most temperature settings. Finally, as <a href="#Sx2.F4" title="In Principle 5: Small-World ‣ Macro-Level Principles ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows, the relation <math id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L\sim\log(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L\sim\log(n)</annotation></semantics></math> holds for different LLM models and environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.SSSx2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">In conclusion, our analysis demonstrates that LLM-generated networks exhibit key small-world properties, with logarithmic scaling of average shortest path lengths and inverse logarithmic scaling of average clustering coefficients. While these networks do not perfectly align with the Watts-Strogatz model, they exhibit similar structural characteristics.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Decisions on Real-World Networks with Heterogeneous Agents</h3>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate the behavior of LLMs in real-world network formation contexts with four datasets in two differing real-world domains.
Despite the significant advancements in social network analysis over recent years, the availability of fully complete and comprehensive network datasets remains exceptionally rare <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite>.
We employ three datasets from the <span id="Sx2.SSx3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Facebook100</span> collection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite> and the telecommunication (<span id="Sx2.SSx3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Andorra</span>) and the employment (<span id="Sx2.SSx3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">MobileD</span>) datasets from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite>. The Facebook100 data correspond to “friendship” networks from one hundred American colleges and universities, captured at a specific moment from Facebook’s online social network. The Andorra dataset contains nationwide call records in Andorra from July 2015 to June 2016, where calls correspond to mutual calls between Andorran residents containing information about the caller’s and the callee’s location, phone type, and usage. Finally, the MobileD dataset corresponds to a company network where relations correspond to call or text communication, and each employee is either a manager or a subordinate.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For all network datasets, the agents have <span id="Sx2.SSx3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">heterogeneous</span> profiles (i.e., profiles with different features) whose statistics (degree distribution, clustering coefficient distribution, assortativity) we report in <a href="#S2.F1" title="In B.1 Statistics of Real-World Datasets ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">SI.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To infer the models’ tendencies, we employ a discrete choice modeling framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>. Specifically, we model the network formation process as a discrete choice process, wherein nodes are sequentially prompted to form connections from a set of available alternatives (see <a href="#S1.SS3.SSS1" title="A.3.1 The Discrete Choice Model in Real-World Network Experiments ‣ A.3 Real-World Network Experiments ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Candidate Set Construction for Network Decisions</h4>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At each decision step <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, a query node <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> selects a link from a set of candidate nodes <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> with size <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|A_{t}|=A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|A_{t}|=A</annotation></semantics></math>. Given the limited context window of LLMs, we consider two alternative strategies for constructing the candidate set <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
</div>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Uniform Sampling.</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We uniformly sample <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> non-neighbor nodes from the graph. This approach serves as a neutral baseline, ensuring that the alternatives presented to the model are selected without structural or feature-based bias. Uniform sampling reflects a scenario where the agent has no <em id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">a priori</em> ranking or filtering of candidates and evaluates all choices purely based on the features provided in the prompt.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Recommendation-Based Sampling.</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also consider a more realistic and structured candidate selection method that mimics the behavior of recommender systems. In this approach, we use a supervised link prediction model based on logistic regression to compute the likelihood of a link between each candidate pair <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,v)</annotation></semantics></math> (cf. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>). The model takes as input common structural features known to be predictive of link formation, such as similarity, the number of common neighbors between <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>, the preferential attachment score between <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>, the Jaccard similarity between the neighborhoods of <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>, and the Adamic-Adar index (see <a href="#S1.SS3.SSS3" title="A.3.3 Candidate Set Construction for Network Decisions ‣ A.3 Real-World Network Experiments ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3.3</span></a> for a description of the recommendation system and <a href="#S2.SS2.SSS1" title="B.2.1 Recommendation System Parameters ‣ B.2 Robustness of Results to Sampling Strategies ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2.1</span></a> for the effect sizes and AUC of the recommendation system). We then select the top-<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> highest-scoring nodes as the candidate set <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> for each query node <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. This method mirrors how real-world systems (e.g., social media friend suggestions, hiring portals, content feeds) narrow down decision spaces through algorithmic filtering based on network and user features.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hyperparameters.</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the three datasets from Facebook100 are Caltech36 (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=769" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>769</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=769</annotation></semantics></math>) Swarthmore42 (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=1,659" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1,659</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=1,659</annotation></semantics></math>), and UChicago30 (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=6,591" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6,591</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=6,591</annotation></semantics></math>), we set the number of alternatives to be <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=15</annotation></semantics></math> and randomly sampled from the existing network. For the UChicago30 dataset, we consider a randomly sampled subset of <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=2,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=2,000</annotation></semantics></math> nodes because of the limited context window of the LLM models. For Andorra (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=32,812" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32,812</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=32,812</annotation></semantics></math>) and MobileD (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=1,982" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1,982</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=1,982</annotation></semantics></math>), we set the number of alternatives to <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=5</annotation></semantics></math> and consider a randomly sampled subset of <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx1.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=1,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=1,000</annotation></semantics></math> nodes.</p>

<td id="Sx2.T1.2.46.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="Sx2.T1.2.46.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">1.05*** (0.007)</span></td>
<td id="Sx2.T1.2.46.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="Sx2.T1.2.46.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">0.36*** (0.005)</span></td>
<td id="Sx2.T1.2.46.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="Sx2.T1.2.46.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">-1,468.61</span></td>
<td id="Sx2.T1.2.46.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="Sx2.T1.2.46.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">2,945.22</span></td></tr>
<tr id="Sx2.T1.2.47" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="Sx2.T1.2.47.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" colspan="6"><em id="Sx2.T1.2.47.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:50%;">Note: *: <math id="Sx2.T1.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.05</annotation></semantics></math>, **: <math id="Sx2.T1.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, ***: <math id="Sx2.T1.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math></em></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:50%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Effect sizes for real-world networks from Facebook100 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>, the Andorra dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite>, and the MobileD dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite> for several LLMs for temperature set to 0.5. We test two sampling strategies: a <span id="Sx2.T1.21" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">uniform</span> strategy where <math id="Sx2.T1.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is sampled uniformly from the set of nodes, and a <span id="Sx2.T1.22" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">recommender system</span> (RecSys) based on logistic regression and trained on pairwise node similarities and network characteristics (number of common neighbors, Jaccard similarity, preferential attachment score, and the Adamic-Adar index). See <a href="#S1.SS3.SSS3" title="A.3.3 Candidate Set Construction for Network Decisions ‣ A.3 Real-World Network Experiments ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3.3</span></a> for more information on the sampling strategies. Average marginal effects (cf. <a href="#S2.SS2.SSS3" title="B.2.3 Average Marginal Effects ‣ B.2 Robustness of Results to Sampling Strategies ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2.3</span></a>) show that homophily is the strongest driver of link formation, with recommendation-based sampling amplifying the dominant mechanism in each dataset while preserving the overall ranking of behavioral factors.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx2.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2402.10659v7/models_comparison.png" id="Sx2.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:429/537;" width="429" height="537" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="Sx2.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison between the network formation decisions among different models for the uniform and the recommendation system sampling strategies</span>. We report the Spearman correlation between the effects corresponding to the fits as well as the total variation (TV) distance between the corresponding fitted models (cf. <a href="#S1.SS3.SSS4" title="A.3.4 Measuring Alignment Between Models ‣ A.3 Real-World Network Experiments ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3.4</span></a> for a detailed description of the metrics).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Regression Coefficients and Model Alignment</h4>

<section id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Uniform Sampling.</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We regress network formation decisions on standardized scores reflecting the three micro-level principles. We present the regression results in <a href="#Sx2.T1" title="In Hyperparameters. ‣ Candidate Set Construction for Network Decisions ‣ Decisions on Real-World Networks with Heterogeneous Agents ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup>
                  <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>
                  
                  
                  
                  
                  
                  
                  
                More detailed results can be found in <a href="#S2.SS3.SSS1" title="B.3.1 Regression Coefficients ‣ B.3 Robustness of Results to Temperature ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3.1</span></a>.</span></span></span> First, we observe a dominant effect of homophily across all datasets and models. The coefficients for homophily (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}</annotation></semantics></math>) are consistently the largest and highly significant (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.05</annotation></semantics></math>) in almost all cases. For instance, in the Caltech36 dataset, the homophily coefficients for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Llama 3 70b Instruct are 0.65, 1.95, and 2.43, respectively (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>). The emphasis on homophily suggests that LLMs, much like humans, prioritize forming connections based on shared characteristics.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Second, we find that preferential attachment plays a secondary role in the network formation decisions of LLMs. While the coefficients for preferential attachment (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{PA}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>PA</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{PA}}</annotation></semantics></math>) are generally positive and statistically significant across most models and datasets, they are notably smaller than those for homophily. For example, in the Swarthmore42 dataset, GPT-3.5 and Llama 3 70b Instruct have preferential attachment coefficients of 0.19 and 0.39, respectively (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>). This suggests that while LLMs do consider the degree of potential connection nodes–favoring connections to well-connected nodes–the influence of this factor is less evident compared to homophily.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The influence of triadic closure appears to vary across different datasets and models. In most cases, the coefficients for triadic closure (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{TC}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>TC</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{TC}}</annotation></semantics></math>) are positive and significant, indicating that LLMs consider the number of mutual connections when forming new links. However, in some instances, such as with GPT-3.5 on the Andorra dataset, the triadic closure coefficient is negative (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.24" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.24</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.24</annotation></semantics></math>) and significant, suggesting a structure-dependent role of this principle as shown by the low clustering coefficient of the network, which is dominated by preferential attachment (cf. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="B.1 Statistics of Real-World Datasets ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>).
This variability implies that while triadic closure is a factor in LLMs’ decision-making, its impact may be influenced by the specific characteristics of the dataset or the model used.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, in <a href="#S2.SS4" title="B.4 Robustness of Results to Large Context Windows ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a> we report the results for larger context windows (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A\in\{50,100\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>50,100</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A\in\{50,100\}</annotation></semantics></math>), and find that our results are robust to larger context windows.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, our analysis demonstrates that while homophily, triadic closure, and preferential attachment are integral to the network formation behaviors of LLMs, homophily is the dominant factor.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Recommendation-Based Sampling and Model Alignment.</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#Sx2.F5" title="In Hyperparameters. ‣ Candidate Set Construction for Network Decisions ‣ Decisions on Real-World Networks with Heterogeneous Agents ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we present both the Spearman correlations of these effects and the total variation (TV) distances between the distributions of agent decisions under the fitted discrete choice models (see <a href="#S1.SS3.SSS3" title="A.3.3 Candidate Set Construction for Network Decisions ‣ A.3 Real-World Network Experiments ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3.3</span></a> for details on the comparison metrics).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis reveals that the key behavioral patterns of LLM agents, namely, the relative strength of their preferences for homophily, triadic closure, and preferential attachment, are largely consistent across different candidate selection strategies. Specifically, we observe high Spearman correlations and low TV distances in the majority of comparisons, both when using the same sampling strategy and when comparing the uniform sampling method to the recommendation-based approach. Homophily still remains the dominant factor in the agent’s decisions and is context-dependent even when the agents interact with the recommendation system.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These results suggest that the observed LLM behaviors are, in the majority, robust to variations in how the candidate set <math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is constructed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Average Marginal Effects.</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to space constraints, we report the average marginal effects (AMEs) in <a href="#S2.SS2.SSS3" title="B.2.3 Average Marginal Effects ‣ B.2 Robustness of Results to Sampling Strategies ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2.3</span></a>. The AMEs provide a complementary view of the regression results by quantifying the expected change in choice probability associated with a one-unit change in each standardized feature. Consistent with the coefficient estimates, homophily exhibits the largest AMEs in most datasets, often exceeding 1.0 and reaching above 2.5 under the recommendation-based strategy (e.g., GPT-4 Mini on UChicago30). Preferential attachment also shows consistently positive AMEs, though typically smaller in magnitude than those for homophily, indicating a weaker, yet still significant, propensity to connect to high-degree nodes. Triadic closure effects are more variable: in several Facebook100 networks they are positive, reinforcing local clustering, while in datasets such as Andorra and MobileD they are frequently negative, indicating a tendency to form cross-community links rather than closing triangles. Across datasets, the recommendation-based strategy tends to amplify the dominant mechanism, i.e., most often homophily in Facebook100 networks and preferential attachment in MobileD, highlighting that sampling strategy can strengthen the prevailing behavioral bias while leaving the relative ranking of mechanisms broadly consistent.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Change of Graph Statistics.</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, the networks resulting from the newly added links preserve the graph statistics (cf. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>), such as the degree distribution, the adjacency matrix spectrum, and the distribution of the sizes of the connected components (see <a href="#S2.SS2.SSS2" title="B.2.2 Change in Graph Statistics due to Different Sampling Strategies ‣ B.2 Robustness of Results to Sampling Strategies ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2.2</span></a> and <a href="#S2.SS3.SSS2" title="B.3.2 Change in Graph Statistics due to Different Temperatures ‣ B.3 Robustness of Results to Temperature ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3.2</span></a>). KS test results show that adding these new edges (<math id="Sx2.SSx3.SSSx2.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 5\%</annotation></semantics></math> new edges) minimally affects global metrics – degree distribution, spectrum, and component sizes remain largely unchanged – while significant shifts occur mainly in local clustering, especially under the Uniform strategy. The Recommendation System produces even fewer local changes, indicating that LLM-driven edge additions at this scale largely preserve overall network structure, with strategy choice shaping only localized patterns. The results are also robust to temperature changes (cf. <a href="#S2.SS3.SSS2" title="B.3.2 Change in Graph Statistics due to Different Temperatures ‣ B.3 Robustness of Results to Temperature ‣ B Real-World Datasets ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3.2</span></a>)</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx2.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.10659v7/human_baseline.svg" id="Sx2.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:429/400;" width="429" height="400"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span><span id="Sx2.F6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Measurement of LLM-Human alignment for two contexts: Social network (<math id="Sx2.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=100)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">𝐎𝐏𝐄𝐍</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=100)</annotation></semantics></math>, and company network (<math id="Sx2.F6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=103" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>103</mn></mrow><annotation
