contains detailed information on the construction of the baseline.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Human Baseline</h3>

<section id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Survey.</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To assess how closely the network formation preferences of LLM agents align with human decision-making, we conducted a controlled survey-based experiment involving both human participants and LLMs. The experiment was designed to elicit link formation choices in two distinct social contexts: <span id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i)</span> a social network where participants assumed the role of a student forming friendships within a college social network, and <span id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii)</span> a company network where participants assumed the role of an employee making professional connections within a company network.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each scenario, the participant was presented with a focal node (representing themselves) and <math id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=3</annotation></semantics></math> candidate profiles containing a value indicating similarity as well as relevant network statistics (degree, common neighbors) with the focal profile. The participant was then asked to select exactly one candidate with whom to form a connection and rate the criteria – among similarity, degree, and common neighbors – that they considered when choosing the specific profile. <a href="#S1.SS4" title="A.4 Human Baseline ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a> contains more information about the experimental setup.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We recruited human participants via the Prolific platform, ensuring diversity in demographic backgrounds. We obtain <math id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=100</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=103" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>103</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=103</annotation></semantics></math> responses for the social and company network contexts, respectively. To compare with LLM models, we administered the same dynamically-generated survey inputs that we gave to each participant to an LLM – preserving the wording, structure, and candidate attributes – for the five LLM models.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This experimental design allows for a direct, context-controlled comparison between human and LLM decision patterns. By presenting an identical set of alternatives, we can measure alignment in two complementary ways: <span id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i)</span> at the <em id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">principle level</em>, by estimating discrete choice models for both humans and LLMs and comparing the inferred effect sizes for homophily, triadic closure, and preferential attachment, and <span id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii)</span> at the <em id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">choice level</em>, by comparing the Borda count vectors between how the participants ranked each criterion in their choices. Furthermore, the two scenarios are chosen to reflect socially and professionally relevant settings as in the case of the real-world datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM-Human Alignment in Network Formation Contexts.</h5>

<div id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#Sx2.F6" title="In Change of Graph Statistics. ‣ Regression Coefficients and Model Alignment ‣ Decisions on Real-World Networks with Heterogeneous Agents ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> summarizes the results of our alignment study. Across all scenarios, the rankings of network formation principles based on effect sizes are perfectly correlated between humans and LLMs, and the Borda vector averages are likewise almost perfectly correlated (with the exception of Claude 3.5). The total variation (TV) distances between the discrete choice models inferred from human and LLM choices are consistently small – below <math id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.32</annotation></semantics></math> in all cases and typically below <math id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.10</annotation></semantics></math> – indicating high distributional similarity (cf. panels (a)-(c)). In the vast majority of cases, the signs of the estimated effects also match between humans and LLMs. Consistent with our earlier observations in <a href="#Sx2.T1" title="In Hyperparameters. ‣ Candidate Set Construction for Network Decisions ‣ Decisions on Real-World Networks with Heterogeneous Agents ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we find strong homophily in the social network context (<math id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}&gt;0;P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>;</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}&gt;0;P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>) and strong heterophily in the company network context (<math id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}&lt;0;P&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>;</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}&lt;0;P&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>). Additionally, the ranking of the effects is consistent with our findings in <a href="#Sx2.T1" title="In Hyperparameters. ‣ Candidate Set Construction for Network Decisions ‣ Decisions on Real-World Networks with Heterogeneous Agents ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While aggregate-level alignment between human and LLM decisions is high across models (cf. <a href="#Sx2.F6" title="In Change of Graph Statistics. ‣ Regression Coefficients and Model Alignment ‣ Decisions on Real-World Networks with Heterogeneous Agents ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>a-c), notable differences emerge in <em id="Sx2.SSx4.SSSx2.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">within-model</em> agreement. Specifically, LLMs exhibit substantially higher internal consistency in their decision rankings than humans, who display greater variability in their within-model rankings (cf. <a href="#Sx2.F6" title="In Change of Graph Statistics. ‣ Regression Coefficients and Model Alignment ‣ Decisions on Real-World Networks with Heterogeneous Agents ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>d).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Discussion</h2>

<section id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Summary of Findings and Broader Impact</h4>

<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this study, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs’ network formation preferences, examining both micro-level network principles–such as preferential attachment, triadic closure, and homophily–and macro-level network properties like community structure and the small-world phenomenon. Our findings indicate that networks generated by multiple LLMs exhibit these properties, particularly when the models are primed with network statistics like the number of mutual friends or the degrees of potential connections.
Furthermore, using discrete choice modeling, we explored the emergence of these properties in simulations based on real-world networks. Our results reveal that the LLM agents’ selections are predominantly driven by homophily, followed by triadic closure and preferential attachment.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">On the one hand, our study enhances our understanding of how multiple LLMs behave in networked settings. Specifically, our findings reveal varying strengths in network formation properties among LLMs, suggesting that when these models are employed to coordinate social networks in social or work environments, they may exhibit human-like behaviors. This has important implications for applications like agent-based modeling, where a realistic simulation of human behavior is crucial.
Traditionally, agent-based models rely on “formalized” rules or heuristics to represent individual behaviors, which may not adequately capture the complexity of human decision-making. Given the abilities of LLMs to solve complex tasks that require extensive reasoning, which may be beyond the scope of a traditional agent-based modeling framework, LLM agents provide the potential to simulate more nuanced and context-aware interactions that can potentially resemble human social behavior closely without the need to specify decision rules or heuristics rigidly.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, our work expands and provides several novel results to the existing literature of findings on LLM-based network simulations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, and is the first, to the best of our knowledge, to include a human baseline to verify the findings. Specifically, in our work, we show the emergence of <em id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">several topological collective biases</em>, which are complementary to the linguistic social conventions found in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, and the emergence of the friendship paradox on LLM-generated networks, as shown in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Limitations and Boundary Conditions</h4>

<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, our results suggest that we should exercise caution when leveraging LLMs in networking scenarios. The model family, configuration, and prompts can subtly affect the models’ behavior, resulting in qualitatively similar but quantitatively different outcomes.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For example, newer models such as GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 exhibit stronger biases compared to prior models such as GPT-3.5. For instance, in the preferential attachment principle, newer models such as GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 have stronger biases – i.e., connect to <span id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">highest</span>-degree-nodes yielding star-like networks – compared to GPT-3.5 and LLama 3, which had weaker biases – i.e., connect to <span id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">high</span>-degree-nodes. Similar results can be found in homophily, as larger biases towards homophily and triadic closure. Thus, even though LLMs exhibit these principles, we should be cautious of such biases when designing simulations.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Similarly, in our experiments with real-world data, we find an interesting phase transition from homophily to heterophily: In the Facebook100 data, the LLMs generally exhibited positive biases toward homophily (<math id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>). However, in employment networks, agents were either managers or subordinates, and we discovered that LLM agents were heterophilous in such a case (<math id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>θ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{H}}&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>), which aligns with career advancement dynamics (i.e., employees want to form links with managers because of better career prospects).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, even though on aggregate LLM and human responses are aligned, the fine-grained picture on the individual level is different: When compared to human responses, the responses given by LLMs are significantly more correlated than the responses obtained by humans (cf. <a href="#Sx2.F6" title="In Change of Graph Statistics. ‣ Regression Coefficients and Model Alignment ‣ Decisions on Real-World Networks with Heterogeneous Agents ‣ Results ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The above underscores the need for researchers to provide oversight and ensure that LLM behaviors align with human expectations when employing them in scientific research methods, such as agent-based modeling and even prototypical human subject research with LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, although we find that LLMs resemble human network formation behaviors, we should consider whether these models should exhibit such behaviors when serving as assistants to humans in work and social lives. Biases like homophily, triadic closure, or preferential attachment may lead to network structures that overemphasize certain individuals or fragment information flow.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, when used as social assistants, LLMs may not necessarily need to mirror human networking behaviors and could be personalized to promote more equitable and efficient information dissemination. Our study highlights the need for more deliberate efforts to align LLM behavior in this domain.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Future Research Directions</h4>

<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Looking ahead, we identify three promising directions for future research: First, investigating LLM behavior in more complex interactions, such as simulated dialogues, could provide deeper insights. By examining the specific dialogues of LLMs during interactions, we can better understand their network formation preferences and how they adapt to different social dynamics.
Second, we could explore how LLMs can be integrated into real-world settings, such as social media platforms. LLM-assisted bots might be employed to facilitate interactions, break echo chambers, and moderate democratic discussions (see, for example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">An important direction for future work is to more explicitly integrate the synthetic and empirical analyses. While our current study shows that the same micro-level principles (homophily, triadic closure, preferential attachment) emerge across both settings, a systematic structural comparison would further validate external robustness. For instance, one can quantify the similarity of LLM-generated synthetic graphs and empirical benchmarks using metrics such as degree distribution, clustering coefficient, assortativity, modularity, or spectral properties. Moreover, causal inference techniques (e.g., counterfactual link removal or intervention-based analyses) could help identify whether the same underlying mechanisms explain network growth in both idealized and real-world scenarios. Such approaches would not only improve interpretability but also establish stronger guarantees that LLM-driven behaviors generalize beyond controlled synthetic environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx4.SSSx3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we can use our methods to create realistic synthetic networks. These synthetic datasets can serve as benchmarks for evaluating graph learning methods, thereby addressing the scarcity of existing graph benchmarks (cf. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>). By adjusting parameters like temperature and environmental settings or selecting different models, we can generate diverse networks to test graph neural network performance under various conditions. Importantly, our approach allows for the generation of artificial data that resembles real-world data while adhering to privacy regulations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx3.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">

<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:207%;">Supplementary Material for 
<br class="ltx_break">“Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs</span></p>
<p id="p1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:120%;">Marios Papachristou<span id="footnote10" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote10.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:83%;">10</span></span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <span id="footnote10.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:83%;">Correspondence to: mpapachr@asu.edu</span></span></span></span>, Yuan Yuan</span></p>
</div>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">A </span>Methods and Materials</h2>

<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Experimental Procedure</h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In our study, we performed experiments to assess whether key network principles at both the micro-level (such as preferential attachment, triadic closure, and homophily) and the macro-level (including community structure and weak ties) align with classical network models. Subsequently, we utilized real-world networks to determine the factors that are most heavily weighted by LLMs.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.1.1 </span>Network Formation Process</h4>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments span a time series of <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> steps, with a sequence of network structures denoted as <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{1},G_{2},\dots,G_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{1},G_{2},\dots,G_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> with vertex sets <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{1},\dots,V_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{1},\dots,V_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>. The initial network, <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, is referred to as the <em id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">seed network</em>. At each step <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, we select a <em id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">query node</em> <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (which may either be a new arrival or an existing node in the graph) and assign it the task of forming new links. This is accomplished by selecting nodes from a set of alternatives <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (meaning potential candidates for link formation) and initiating a query call <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}(A_{t},i_{t},\delta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}(A_{t},i_{t},\delta)</annotation></semantics></math> to the LLM (as outlined in <a href="#alg2" title="In A.1.2 Prompts ‣ A.1 Experimental Procedure ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">SI.2</span></a>) to create up to <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math> new links. The edge set selection process involves presenting the LLMs with personal or network features of the alternatives, denoted as <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(A_{t})=\left\{f_{a}:a\in A_{t}\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(A_{t})=\left\{f_{a}:a\in A_{t}\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>, which may include information such as the neighbors of the nodes, node degrees, common connections with <math id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and community memberships, formatted in JSON. We adopt a zero-shot learning approach, avoiding the provision of examples to the model to prevent bias, in line with relevant studies such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>. This approach allows for the exploration of the innate preferences of LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We employ multiple temperatures to account for the variability in response generation by LLM systems, which is also observed in classical statistical models of network formation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. Our study conducts experiments using three temperatures for all models except Claude 3.5: 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5. For Claude 3.5 the temperature range is between 0 and 1, and we run experiments with two temperatures: 0.5, and 1.0.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, the model is tasked with outputting a JSON object indicating the node chosen for link formation and the rationale behind the choice. This approach is adopted because LLMs have demonstrated proficiency in processing code-like structures, such as HTML and JSON.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.1.2 </span>Prompts</h4>

<div id="S1.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The general prompt we use is given in <a href="#alg2" title="In A.1.2 Prompts ‣ A.1 Experimental Procedure ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">SI.2</span></a>. An example of this prompt is given at <a href="#alg1" title="In A.1.2 Prompts ‣ A.1 Experimental Procedure ‣ A Methods and Materials ‣ Network Formation and Dynamics among Multi-LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">SI.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>

</div>
